desc:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order and has at least two elements. Among all sums nums[i] + nums[j] with i < j, return the sum that is closest to target (smallest absolute difference).

If two different sums are equally close, return the smaller of them. Return the sum itself, not the positions.

nums = [1, 3, 8, 10, 15], target = 12
sums 11 (=1+10 or 3+8) and 13 (=3+10) are both at distance 1
result = 11
hints: Trying every pair works but takes O(n²). Use the sorted order.
Look at the smallest and the largest element. If their sum is below the target, can the smallest element do better with a partner other than the largest one?

Keep two pointers at the ends. Record the current sum if it beats the best one (closer, or equally close and smaller). Move lo right when the sum is below the target, hi left when above, and stop immediately on equality.
editorial: Set lo = 0, hi = n - 1. At each step look at s = a[lo] + a[hi] and compare it with the best sum so far using the key (|s - target|, s), which also encodes the tie rule. If s == target nothing can be closer, so return it.

If s < target, the element at lo combined with any partner at or before hi gives a sum at most s, which is even further below the target, so lo can be discarded. Symmetrically, when s > target the element at hi is discarded. Each step removes one index: O(n) time and O(1) space.
The same discard argument is the engine of 3Sum, 4Sum and their closest-sum variants: fix some elements, then sweep the rest with two pointers.
